messages.subject: Help beach transects
parts:
Hello, 

I'm trying to develop a I am trying to develop a methodology for estimating the abundance and density of litter on beaches.
I want a 100m beach section and then I was doing 20 zigzag 5 meter transects (sketch of the transects attached) arranged diagonally along the beach section to get all the garbage density gradients (from the top from the beach to the low tide line).

Is it possible to make zigzag transects and establish a maximum detection distance (truncate the distances in the field) to about 5 m for example?
 
In practice the length of my transects (or radial) would be more than 5m, would be about 7 meters (because we are walking diagonally). (But the main transect or the guiding medium line would be 100m)

How can I set a random start point?

I also attached a detection probability function that I did with data from a beach test. The obtained shoulder means that we were detecting too much up to the maximum distance established  (width), right


Thanks in advance,

Sara

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
parts:
Hi Sara

Your design sketch looks pretty good.  Answers to your specific questions:

a) yes, you can truncate distances in the field.  However, if you have transects 5m long, I would not truncate at 5m, because that will lead to large areas of overlap in coverage areas between legs of the zigzag. Simply sketch out a box that is 10m wide centred on each of your transect legs to see what I mean.  If you want your transects to be 5m in length, then perhaps your truncation distance might be only 2m.  Even then there will be overlap in coverage areas between consecutive legs.  You should create a decision rule about what to do with the overlap areas.  To which leg should those overlapping areas belong?

Have a look a the lecture describing this issue on our new online course:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#design-of-distance-sampling-surveys (slides 12 and 13 of that lecture).

b) To create a random start, choose a random number between 0 and 100.  Start the first leg of your zigzag at that location along your "guiding medium line".  Lay your zigzag legs from there until you have your 20 legs, or until you run into the sea.  If you run into the sea before finishing your 20 legs, allocate the remaining legs starting at distance 0 (in this case you will have some of your legs near the sea and the remainder of legs near the beach top with a gap in effort in between).

c) The fitted detection function you sent suggests that detectability does not drop off very rapidly as a function of distance.  You appear to still be seeing ~80% of the objects out at your 5m truncation distance.  The overall proportion of objects you see within the truncation distance is ~90%.  There is nothing horrible about that.

I do wonder about the size of your pieces of litter relative to the scale of your measurements.  If the litter is bottles, they are small relative to the width of the cutpoints in the histogram.  However, if the litter is sheets of plastic or pieces of rope (often the type of beach litter we see here in Scotland), then it the rope can be >1m in length.  If so, what is the distance to the transect you are recording?  If you measure its closest distance, perhaps that is the explanation for the "spike" in the first distance bin.  I would suggest the better distance to record would be the average distance from the rope to the transect; more precisely the distance from the "centre" of the rope to the transect.  Have a look at this online lecture to see the concept described in context of groups of animals:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter4/#field-methods (slide 11)

messages.author: 0ebfa823f5ba1c0a
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
parts:
Hello Eric,

Thank you again for the advice and answers! I think this group is a very important space for those using this method, and your willingness to respond and help is to be praised.

We decided to change the approach of beach transects to prevent these large areas of overlap in coverage areas between legs of the zigzag. So, we tried a design of 20 transects of 10 meters in a straight line, also equally spaced by 10 meters, which would give an area of: 400m length x width of the beach. In this way we would not have this overlap problem.

We measured the width of the beach at the beginning and divided by 2, and there was the beginning of the transect.

The results of the analyzes surprised me, I think it resulted in good detection probability curves, and low coefficients of variation. The only drawback is with larger size classes (class L and XL) that do not have a probability of detection = 1 in the transect line. Most of these objects were furthest from the transect line. Do you think this will be a problem if we take this method?

size L: between 10 cm and 1m
size XL: > 1m

I did several analyzes, one analysis without any truncation, another with a truncation of 5% of the largest distances, analyzes by size classes (with and without truncation), and analyzes with truncation at 20 meters distance.

In wider beaches, we were thinking of doing 2 lines of 10 transects of 10m side by side, and a continuous line of 20 transects of 10m on the narrowest beaches.

I would really appreciate if you could see the analyzes of this test we did, and say if there is something that is not working, or is there any parameter that should be better? Any suggestions. I'll send the project by email, ok?

Once more, thank you for the help,

Sara

parts:
Hi Sara,

Just a couple of points:

1. I would not have the transects parallel to the coast line, but perpendicular to the coast line, to avoid density gradients (I wonder if this is somehow related to the second problem). As you have it you are oversampling some areas which are not random with respect to litter distribution.
2. It seems weird that g(0) is not 1 for the largest classes. Since g(0) is the probability of detecting an object on the line, I would expect it to be lower for the smaller classes?

Any way, maybe this is a discussion to have off the list.

cheers

Tiago

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
parts:
Yes, as Tiago says, lines should not be parallel to the shoreline.  Your design creates two major problems.  First, your design is a single line with gaps, not replicate lines, so variance estimates will be invalidated.  (For wider beaches, you would have 2 lines.)  Second, objects will not be uniformly distributed with respect to distance from the line.  You see this with your large objects, which are relatively unlikely to be recorded in the middle of the beach I imagine.  You’re interpreting the distribution of distances from the line as if it reflects probability of detection, but it is more likely that it largely reflects varying density of objects as you move up the beach.

 

I think you should either have transects along the beach and attempt complete counts (possibly with gaps as per your design, and possibly using more than one observer walking line abreast) or have lines perpendicular to the shore line, and use distance sampling.  If the latter, decide what is a reasonable truncation distance.  If you adopt say 20m, then put the lines a minimum of 40m apart, and for each line, record anything detected within 20m of the line.  Ideally each line will run from the top of the beach to the low water mark.

 

This may be impractical, but your design will not yield valid analysis, so a different compromise may need to be found.

 

Steve Buckland

Hello, 

Thank you so much for your advice and suggestions. 

We decided to use distance sampling with 10 lines perpendicular to the shore line, from the top of the beach to the high tide line. The lines were placed a minimum of 40m apart, and for each line, anything detected within 20m of the line was recorded. The area was the same: 400m length x width of the beach.

Regarding the results, in the first general analysis I did, the g(0)of the detection function isn't =1.

Post-stratifying the data by size class:

size L: g(0)=1 which is good

size M: g(0) is near 1, but it isn't 1

size S: g(0) is not 1,

size XL: g(0) is not 1. but this size class has very few observations.

So, I did an experimental analysis by color (although I have to simplify this categories yet), because we detected frequently blue/green/red S sized objects till 9 or 10 meters maybe. But in the analysis, the white and blue itens weren't both also not g(0)=1.

Or maybe, it can be related to the fact that marine litter distribution doesn't have a specific distribution. In some beaches it can be more acumulated on the strandline or at the top at the beach but in others it can be a little more random. What do you think?

I have a question:  As I get more beaches sampled and analyzed, I also get more data about my ability to detect objects. Can I, after having all my beaches sampled, get an overall analysis with an overall detection function curve with all my data?
I send my distance project attached.

Size Classes:

S: >0,5 <2,5 cm
M: >2,5 <10 cm
L: >10 <1 m
XL: >1m


Thank you again for the opportunity to improve my work.

Best wishes, 

Sara Sá

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
parts:
Sara

A few comments about what you have sent.

- I would think that you should see all objects >1m in size; I would treat that category as a strip transect.

- Your assessment of g(0) for your size categories, I presume are based upon visual inspection of the histograms produced by Distance.  I think that is a bit misleading.  This histogram for your M-class does not look bad to me

mere stochasticity can produce the bumpiness shown in this histogram; that does not necessarily imply g(0)<1.

- The histogram above, as well as that for class S indicate the need to truncate your data considerably before fitting detection functions.  I'd suggest truncation perhaps around 12m for M and perhaps 5m for S.

- I have nothing useful to say about spatial distribution of litter on beaches.

- You have lots of detections per beach and size, so I don't see much advantage to combining data (hence detection functions) across beaches.  You may wish to entertain the possibility that detection functions differ between beaches by keeping the data separate.
